# Introduction

In this section, we show how to reshape data from long to wide (and vice versa). We do this for both raw and cleaned data. To demonstrate, we use data on cohort members' height and weight collected in Sweeps 8 and 9 (ages 25 and 32).

# Reshaping Raw Data from Wide to Long

We begin by loading the data from each sweep and merging these together into a single wide format dataset; see [Combining Data Across Sweeps](https://cls-data.github.io/data-handling-stata/docs/next_steps-merging_across_sweeps.html) for further explanation on how this is achieved. Height and weight are stored in the main interview files for Sweeps 8 and 9 (`ns8_2015_main_interview.dta` and `ns9_2022_main_interview.dta`, both in the `safeguarded_eul` subfolder). The names of the height and weight variables follow the same convention in the two sweeps, differing only in the prefix that denotes the sweep (`W8HEIGHT` and `W9HEIGHT`; `W8WEIGHT` and `W9WEIGHT`). This is typical for variables collected in Sweeps 8 and 9, but [not for variables collected in both earlier and later sweeps](https://cls-data.github.io/data-handling-stata/docs/next_steps-data_structures.html), which usually need to be renamed before they can be reshaped. Below, `order` and `sort` are used to arrange the columns and rows of the merged dataset.

```{stata}
use NSID W8HEIGHT W8WEIGHT using "safeguarded_eul/ns8_2015_main_interview.dta", clear
save "temp_w8.dta", replace

use NSID W9HEIGHT W9WEIGHT using "safeguarded_eul/ns9_2022_main_interview.dta", clear
merge 1:1 NSID using "temp_w8.dta", nogenerate
order NSID W8HEIGHT W8WEIGHT W9HEIGHT W9WEIGHT
sort NSID
list in 1/10
```

The dataset has 5 variables. Besides the identifier, `NSID`, there are 4 variables for height and weight measurements at each sweep. Each of these 4 variables is prefixed by the letter `W` and a single digit indicating the sweep. We can reshape the dataset into long format (one row per person x sweep combination) using the `reshape long` command so that the resulting dataset has four variables: one person identifier, a variable for sweep, and variables for height and weight. By default, `reshape long` expects the variables that are to be reshaped to be named in a specific format: `stub` + `suffix`.[^1] Here, we want our stubs to be `HEIGHT` and `WEIGHT`, and our suffixes to be the sweep numbers (8 and 9). As the sweep number is currently towards the start of the variable names, we first rename the variables to match this format. In the `rename` command, `#` is a wildcard that stands for one or more digits, so `W8HEIGHT` is renamed `HEIGHT8`, `W9HEIGHT` is renamed `HEIGHT9`, and so on. Then in the `reshape long` command, we specify the stubs in the main command, with the identifier and suffix variables specified in the `i()` and `j()` command options respectively. Note the identifier (`i()`) exists in the data, while the suffix variable (`j()`) is created during the reshape process.

[^1]: The position of the suffix can instead be marked with an `@` in the stub. For instance, `reshape long W@HEIGHT W@WEIGHT, i(NSID) j(sweep)` would reshape the data without the variables being renamed first, though the reshaped variables would then be named `WHEIGHT` and `WWEIGHT`.

```{stata}
rename (W#HEIGHT W#WEIGHT) (HEIGHT# WEIGHT#) // Moves the sweep number to the end of the name, where reshape expects it by default
reshape long HEIGHT WEIGHT, i(NSID) j(sweep)
list in 1/10
```

Note, when reshaping to long format, multiple variables are effectively appended together, so the reshaped variables can only have one set of value labels. In this case, the value labels attached to the Sweep 8 and Sweep 9 variables are not identical (for instance, `-8` is labelled "Insufficient information" in Sweep 8 and "Don't know" in Sweep 9). `reshape long` does not print a warning about this. It keeps the value labels of one variable in each set (here, those of the Sweep 9 variables), so values from Sweep 8 are displayed with the Sweep 9 labels, and the original labels are not restored if the data are later reshaped back to wide format. Where this is a concern, value labels can be removed before the variables are renamed and reshaped using `label values` (for instance, `label values W8HEIGHT W8WEIGHT W9HEIGHT W9WEIGHT .`).

# Reshaping Raw Data from Long to Wide

We can reshape the data from long to wide format using the `reshape wide` command. We again specify the stubs in the main command, and the identifier and suffix variables in `i()` and `j()`, respectively. The suffix variable exists in the data, and its values are used to create the new variable names during the reshape process. We then use `rename` to return the variables to their original names, with the sweep number following the initial `W`.

```{stata}
reshape wide HEIGHT WEIGHT, i(NSID) j(sweep)
rename (HEIGHT# WEIGHT#) (W#HEIGHT W#WEIGHT)
list in 1/10
```

# Reshaping Cleaned Data from Long to Wide

It is likely that you will not just need to reshape raw data, but cleaned data too. In the next two sections we offer advice on naming variables so that they are easy to select and reshape in long or wide formats. First, we reshape the raw data to long format once more and clean it by creating a new variable for the cohort member's age at each sweep, and creating new `height` and `weight` variables that replace negative values in the raw height and weight data with `.` (as well as giving these variables more easy-to-understand names). To create the age variable, we create a global macro, `ages`, which contains the (approximate) age of cohort members at each of the nine sweeps, and use the `word()` function to pick out the entry for the relevant sweep (i.e., `word("${ages}", 8)` returns `25`). As `word()` returns text, we use `real()` to convert the result to a number. We create the `height` and `weight` variables with `gen double` so that no precision is lost when the values are copied: by default, `gen` creates variables of type `float`, which hold fewer significant digits than variables of type `double`.

```{stata}
global ages 14 15 16 17 18 19 20 25 32

rename (W#HEIGHT W#WEIGHT) (HEIGHT# WEIGHT#)
reshape long HEIGHT WEIGHT, i(NSID) j(sweep)
gen age = real(word("${ages}", sweep))
gen double height = HEIGHT if HEIGHT > 0 // double keeps the full precision of the raw values
gen double weight = WEIGHT if WEIGHT > 0
keep NSID age height weight
list in 1/10
```

To reshape the clean data from long to wide format, we can use the `reshape wide` command as before. This time, we specify the variable containing the cohort member's age in `j()`, so that the new variable names end with the age at measurement (`height25`, `height32`, and so on). We then use `rename` to add an underscore between the stub and the age.

```{stata}
reshape wide height weight, i(NSID) j(age)
rename (height# weight#) (height_# weight_#)
list in 1/10
```

Notice that the new variable names consist of a descriptive stub, an underscore, and the age at measurement (in the output above, `list` shortens the names - `height_25` is displayed as `heigh~25`, for instance). A consistent convention such as this makes it simple to refer to groups of variables using wildcards, either by name (e.g., `height_??`) or by numerical range (e.g., `?eight_2?`).[^2] As cohort members were aged between 14 and 32 in Sweeps 1-9, the age is always two characters long. In studies that include measurements from earlier in life, it is worth padding ages with a leading zero (e.g., `height_05`) so that the names of similar variables are the same length.

[^2]: In `Stata`, `?` is a wildcard that stands for exactly one character and `*` is a wildcard that stands for zero or more characters. `height_??` therefore matches any variable name that begins `height_` and is followed by exactly two characters, while `?eight_2?` matches the height and weight variables measured between ages 20 and 29 (here, `height_25` and `weight_25`).

# Reshaping Cleaned Data from Wide to Long

Finally, we can reshape the clean wide dataset back to long format using the `reshape long` command. As the variable names now include an underscore before the age, we specify the stubs as `height_` and `weight_`, and then use `rename` to remove the underscores from the names of the reshaped variables. Note how easy it is to specify the variables we want to reshape: because we used a consistent naming structure for the cleaned variables, we only need to give `reshape long` the two stubs.

```{stata}
reshape long height_ weight_, i(NSID) j(age)
rename (height_ weight_) (height weight)
list in 1/10
```
